extracted.intended_audience: healthcare industry compliance officers, corporate counsel, and legal professionals monitoring False Claims Act enforcement
extracted.subtask_description: A law-firm alert summarizing the U.S. Department of Justice's False Claims Act (FCA) recoveries, qui tam activity, enforcement priorities, and notable healthcare-related settlements for fiscal year 2024.

rubrics_metrics.name: Total FCA settlements and judgments (FY 2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: On Jan. 15, 2025, the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) announced False Claims Act (FCA) settlements and judgments exceeded $2.9 billion in the fiscal year (FY) ending Sept. 30, 2024; the government and whistleblowers were party to 558 settlements and judgments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative context: FY 2023 settlements and judgments totaled $2.68 billion based on 543 settlements and judgments. Use counts of settlements/judgments and aggregate dollar recoveries to assess enforcement intensity year-to-year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whistleblower (qui tam) filings and recoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Whistleblowers filed 979 qui tam lawsuits in FY 2024 (the highest number ever filed in a single year). Recoveries in whistleblower lawsuits totaled more than $2.4 billion, comprising around 83 percent of all FCA recoveries in FY 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track qui tam filing volume and the dollar share of recoveries from qui tams to gauge the role of whistleblowers in overall enforcement; rising qui tam filings signal increased private enforcement risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Healthcare-related recoveries and significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Matters pertaining to the healthcare industry comprised the largest portion of FCA FY 2024 settlements and judgments: recoveries for healthcare-related matters totaled over $1.67 billion, making up around 58 percent of all recoveries in FY 2024.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify types of healthcare defendants (managed care providers, hospitals, clinics, pharmacies, pharmaceutical companies, laboratories, physicians) when assessing sectoral risk; note slight decrease from FY 2023 ($1.8 billion, ~68%).

rubrics_metrics.name: DOJ enforcement priority topics
rubrics_metrics.description: The DOJ highlighted the opioid epidemic, unnecessary services, substandard care, Medicare Advantage, unlawful kickbacks, Stark Law violations, and COVID-19 related fraud as specific enforcement priorities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this prioritized list to focus internal compliance reviews and risk assessments; these topics represent areas where DOJ will concentrate investigative and enforcement resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opioid-epidemic-related conduct (example of actionable conduct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A now-bankrupt pharmaceutical company agreed the United States retained a claim in the bankruptcy of $475.6 million related to allegations of marketing an opioid drug to high-volume prescribers, including prescribers that the company knew were prescribing the opioid drug for non-medically accepted uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Marketing practices that target high-volume prescribers or encourage off-label/non-medically-accepted uses are enforcement risks under the FCA; promotional conduct should be reviewed for compliance with applicable statutes/regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unnecessary services and substandard care
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A healthcare system and 12 affiliated skilled nursing facilities agreed to pay $21.3 million to resolve allegations that they knowingly billed federal healthcare programs for therapy services that were unreasonable, unnecessary or unskilled, or did not occur as billed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Billing for services that are unreasonable, unnecessary, unskilled, or not rendered can trigger FCA exposure; compliance programs should validate medical necessity, documentation, and billing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medicare Advantage-related kickbacks and recruitment
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A primary care chain paid $60 million to resolve allegations that it paid kickbacks to third-party insurance agents in exchange for recruiting seniors to primary care clinics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compensation/marketing arrangements that reward enrollment/recruitment for Medicare Advantage may be unlawful kickbacks; contracts and referral incentives should be reviewed for anti-kickback and specialty program compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlawful kickbacks and Stark Law referral inducements
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A biopharmaceutical research service provider agreed to pay over $5 million to resolve allegations that it made millions of dollars of commission payments to independent-contractor marketers to induce the marketers to recommend providers refer clinical laboratory orders to the company.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission payments or referral-based compensation that induce clinical referrals risk both anti-kickback statute and Stark Law violations; structure compensation to avoid impermissible referral incentives and document legitimate services.

rubrics_metrics.name: COVID-19-related fraud (testing/kickbacks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A Georgia laboratory owner and the clinical laboratory he owned paid $14.3 million to resolve allegations that they paid kickbacks to independent contractor sales representatives to recommend respiratory pathogen panel tests to senior communities interested only in COVID-19 tests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Targeted testing regimes and kickback-driven test recommendations can produce FCA exposure; confirm commercial arrangements for testing and marketing comply with anti-kickback rules and reflect medical necessity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to report Medicare drug rebates
rubrics_metrics.description: The DOJ reported a national pharmacy chain’s multimillion-dollar settlement to resolve allegations related to failures to report drug rebates to the Medicare program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure accurate reporting of drug rebates and similar obligations to federal healthcare programs; failures to report required information can be the basis for FCA allegations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance recommendation / minimizing FCA liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Takeaway: Healthcare fraud continues to be a leading focus of the DOJ’s enforcement efforts. To minimize potential liability under the FCA, entities in the healthcare industry should consider prioritizing compliance reviews of policies surrounding the government’s enforcement priorities discussed above.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical action: prioritize policy and compliance reviews focused on DOJ-identified priority areas (opioids, unnecessary services, Medicare Advantage, kickbacks, Stark, COVID-19 issues); consider conducting audits, updating policies, and training to address these risks.
